g9-geography-ug3-t1.overview: Natural resources are natural assets occurring in nature that can be used for economic production or consumption. This lesson classifies them into renewable and non-renewable resources and explains the forces degrading Ethiopia's resource base.
objectives: Recognise the concept of natural resources
Classify natural resources into renewable and non-renewable types
Give Ethiopian examples of each resource class
Explain the factors affecting natural resources in Ethiopia
Describe sustainable utilization of natural resources
g9-geography-ug3-t1.simple: Natural resources are natural assets occurring in nature that can be used for economic production or consumption. They are classified into two groups. Renewable resources can be replenished by nature; examples are plants, animals, soil, water, geothermal energy, wind energy and solar radiation. Non-renewable resources cannot be regenerated by nature and exist in limited amounts; examples are all minerals, coal, crude oil and natural gas. In Ethiopia, these resources are influenced by interconnected factors such as population pressure, agricultural expansion, migration, rapid urbanization, resettlement, climate change and environmental pollution. The huge population of Ethiopia puts a great burden on sustainability, so there is serious degradation of land, water, forest, rangeland and wildlife resources, and these degradations feed off each other.
g9-geography-ug3-t1.detailed:
The concept of natural resources. Natural resources are natural assets occurring in nature that can be used for economic production or consumption. They are the foundation of any economic development, food security and other basic necessities for the Ethiopian population. In this unit the major natural resources of Ethiopia are soils, water, natural vegetation and wildlife.

The two great classes. Natural resources are classified into renewable resources and non-renewable resources. Renewable resources are resources which can be replenished by nature. Plants, animals, soil, water, geothermal energy, wind energy and solar radiation are categorized under renewable resources. Non-renewable resources are resources that cannot be regenerated by nature and exist in limited amount; all minerals, coal, crude oil and natural gas belong to this class.

Why the difference matters. A renewable resource can recover if it is given the chance, for example a forest regrows if it is replanted and protected. A non-renewable resource such as crude oil simply becomes scarcer every time it is extracted, because nature cannot replace it on a human time scale. This is why the wise use of non-renewables is a matter of stewardship for future generations.

Factors affecting natural resources in Ethiopia. In Ethiopia these resources are under the influence of various interconnected factors like population pressure, agricultural expansion, migration, rapid urbanization, resettlement, climate change and environmental pollution. Because the factors are interconnected, damage to one resource damages others.

The burden of a huge population. The huge population of Ethiopia had been putting a great burden on the sustainability of almost all types of natural resources. There is, therefore, serious degradation of land, water, forest, rangeland, and wildlife resources that appear to feed off each other: deforestation exposes soil, exposed soil washes into rivers, and wildlife loses its habitat.

Sustainable utilization. Sustainable utilization means using natural resources in a way and at a rate that allows nature to renew them, so that they can serve the present generation without denying the same service to future generations. Forest, soil and water conservation work is the practical response to the degradation described above.

workedExamples.problem: Ethiopia's resource base is under pressure from several forces. Using the textbook list, explain why land degradation spreads once forest resources decline.
workedExamples.given: Ethiopia has serious degradation of land, water, forest, rangeland and wildlife resources that appears to feed off each other.
workedExamples.formula: Method: link the degradation pattern by cause and effect, since the factors are interconnected.
workedExamples.substitution: Forest loss removes vegetation cover; without cover, soil erodes; eroded soil silts water resources and wildlife habitats shrink.
workedExamples.calculation: Following the chain of effects shows that the degradation of one resource intensifies the degradation of the others.

workedExamples.given: Water, solar radiation and animals are listed, together with a mineral (limestone).

workedExamples.problem: A farmer uses crop residues and dung for cooking fuel instead of leaving them on the field. Which resource generation is weakened and why?
workedExamples.given: Soil is classified as a renewable resource, but renewal depends on settled climate, vegetation and modest extraction rates.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a renewable resource stays renewable only while it is replenished faster than it is used up (sustainable utilization).
workedExamples.substitution: Removing residues and dung strips organic matter from the field faster than nature replaces it.
workedExamples.calculation: Extraction rate now exceeds the replenishment rate, so soil fertility declines instead of renewing.
workedExamples.answer: Soil renewal is weakened; the use of organic matter has become unsustainable, turning a renewing soil into a degrading one.

workedExamples.problem: Two towns, one burning coal and one using geothermal and wind energy, plan 100 years of energy supply. Predict the sustainability of each plan.
workedExamples.given: Coal is a non-renewable resource; geothermal energy and wind energy are renewable resources.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: non-renewables exist in limited amount; renewables can be replenished by nature.
workedExamples.substitution: The coal stock only shrinks with use, while geothermal heat and wind keep arriving.
workedExamples.calculation: The coal town exhausts its deposit and must search for another; the geothermal-wind town keeps a lasting supply.
workedExamples.answer: The geothermal and wind plan is sustainable; the coal plan is not, because nature cannot regenerate coal.

g9-geography-ug3-t2.overview: A drainage system describes the flow direction and destination of a country's rivers, and Ethiopia's systems are the result of Cenozoic structural events. This lesson maps the three drainage systems of Ethiopia and their basins.
objectives: Explain what a drainage system is
Describe how the drainage systems of Ethiopia formed
Identify the rivers of each of the three drainage systems
Compare the size and discharge of the three systems
Trace the course of the Awash River from source to end
g9-geography-ug3-t2.simple: Drainage systems refer to the flow direction and destination of rivers. Ethiopia's drainage patterns are the result of various structural events that took place in the Cenozoic era, and the flow is guided by the high rim of plateaus: rivers leave the highlands for the surrounding lowlands and seas. Ethiopia is classified into three major drainage systems. The Western (Mediterranean Sea) system is the largest, covering river Tekezze, Abbay and Baro-Akobo, which join the Nile in Sudan and end in the Mediterranean Sea. The Southeastern (Indian Ocean) system, second largest, is made of the Genale and Wabe Shebelle. The Inland (Rift Valley) system, the smallest, contains the Awash, Omo-Gibe, several lakes and smaller streams.
g9-geography-ug3-t2.detailed:
What a drainage system is. Drainage systems refer to the flow direction and destination of the rivers. The drainage patterns and systems of Ethiopia are the results of various structural events that took place in the Cenozoic era. The natural factor behind them is the relief built by these events: rivers rise on the central highlands and run outward to the peripheral lowlands, so their outward pattern mirrors the shape of the land.

The Western (Mediterranean Sea) drainage system. The system is the largest of the three systems both in terms of catchment area and volume of water, contributing 60% of the country's total annual water discharge. It is made up of three major rivers and their tributaries. River Tekezze drains the Massif of western Lasta, northern Gondar/Semein and southwestern, western and central Tigray. River Abbay has its origin in the Gojjam plateau, and large number of streams join it from the plateaus of western Shewa, southwestern Wollo, northern Wollega and northern Illubabor; it has a semicircular course from Lake Tana, separating southeastern Gondar from Gojjam and separating Gojjam from Shewa. River Baro-Akobo drains the wettest highlands of the southwest, and crosses the border to join the Nile. These river waters join the Nile in Sudan, ending in the Mediterranean Sea.

The Southeastern (Indian Ocean) drainage system. This system is the second largest drainage system and it consists of the Genale and Wabe Shebelle rivers, which collect water from the highlands of Hararghe, Sidamo, Bale and Arsi. The system flows southeast, across the Somali arid and semi-arid areas, and contributes about 32% of the country's total annual water flow. The Wabe Shebelle, the longest river in the country, does not reach the Indian Ocean; it ends at the Benadir coast of Somalia. The Genale, however, reaches the Indian Ocean: it joins the Dawa River at the Ethio-Somalia border, where it acquires the name Juba.

The Inland (Rift Valley) drainage system. This system is the smallest of the three in terms of catchment area, discharge of water and volume of water. There are a number of lakes and smaller streams, like the Bilate and Gedabo, which flow into Lake Abbaya, the Segan, which flows into Chew Bahir, and the Meki and Katar, which flow into Lake Ziway. The major rivers of the system are the Awash and the Omo-Gibe.

The Awash River basin. The Awash river basin is the most utilized in the Rift Valley. The basin covers a total area of 110,000 km2. The river rises from the Shewan plateau near Ginchi town, about 100 kilometers west of Addis Ababa, and flows along the Rift Valley; its middle and lower courses belong to the Great Rift Valley system, though the upper course does not. It terminates in the salty Lake Abbe on the border with Djibouti. The lower Awash basin contains the deltaic alluvial plains of the Tendaho, Assaita and Dit Behri areas, and the terminal lake area.

Why the map matters. Knowing which system a basin belongs to tells a geographer where the water ends up, which countries share each river, and where Ethiopia's unexploited water potential lies. About 8% of annual flow remains in the inland basin, and the biggest flows leave through the western rivers that feed the Nile.

workedExamples.problem: A river rises on the southwestern highlands, leaves Ethiopia, joins the Nile in Sudan and finally ends in the Mediterranean Sea. Which drainage system does it belong to?
workedExamples.given: The river's destination is the Nile in Sudan and the Mediterranean Sea.
workedExamples.formula: Method: classify a river by its flow direction and destination.
workedExamples.substitution: Rivers that join the Nile belong to the Western system, which consists of the Tekezze, Abbay and Baro-Akobo.
workedExamples.calculation: The destination matches the Western system, so the river is Baro-Akobo, not a Rift Valley or Indian Ocean river.
workedExamples.answer: The Western (Mediterranean Sea) drainage system; a southwestern highland river that joins the Nile is Baro-Akobo.

workedExamples.problem: In a data table of rivers: one river is the longest in the country but never reaches the Indian Ocean, ending at the Benadir coast of Somalia. Name the river and the reason.
workedExamples.given: Wabe Shebelle has the greatest length, and the textbook states it does not reach the Indian Ocean.
workedExamples.formula: Method: compare the stated course and end point of a river with the defining property of its drainage system.
workedExamples.substitution: The Wabe Shebelle flows southeast across the Somali arid and semi-arid area and terminates at the Benadir coast.
workedExamples.calculation: Because its water does not reach the sea, it is an inland-ending river inside a sea-directed system.
workedExamples.answer: The Wabe Shebelle; despite belonging to the Indian Ocean system, it dries up and ends inland at the Benadir coast of Somalia.

workedExamples.problem: The three systems contribute 60% (western), 32% (southeastern), and the remainder (inland) of Ethiopia's total annual water discharge. How much water ends in the inland system?
workedExamples.given: Western system contributes 60%, the Southeastern system about 32% of total annual discharge.
workedExamples.formula: Method: the three shares together must sum to 100%.
workedExamples.calculation: The remaining percentage is the share of the inland (Rift Valley) system.
workedExamples.answer: About 8%, confirming that the Inland (Rift Valley) system is the smallest in volume of water.

workedExamples.problem: A map shows the rivers Meki, Katar, Bilate and Gedabo, all ending in Ethiopian lakes rather than the sea. Put these rivers and lakes in their correct drainage arrangement.
workedExamples.given: The Bilate and Gedabo flow into Lake Abbaya; the Meki and Katar flow into Lake Ziway; none leaves the country.
workedExamples.formula: Method: rivers ending inside the country belong to the Inland (Rift Valley) drainage system.
workedExamples.substitution: Both pairs of streams end in Rift Valley lakes, so their flow direction is inward to the Rift Valley floor.
workedExamples.calculation: This places all four streams in the Inland system, alongside the major Awash and Omo-Gibe rivers.
workedExamples.answer: All four belong to the Inland (Rift Valley) drainage system, ending in Lake Abbaya and Lake Ziway.

g9-geography-ug3-t2.summary: Drainage systems describe the flow direction and destination of rivers, and Ethiopia's three systems arise from structural events of the Cenozoic era. The Western system (Tekezze, Abbay, Baro-Akobo) is the largest, carrying 60% of annual discharge to the Nile and the Mediterranean Sea; the Southeastern system (Genale, Wabe Shebelle) carries about 32% toward the Indian Ocean; and the smallest Inland system, with the Awash and Omo-Gibe, ends in Rift Valley lakes such as Abbaya and Ziway.

g9-geography-ug3-t3.overview: Ethiopia is known as the Water Tower of Northeastern Africa and is the second richest African country in water resource potential after the Democratic Republic of Congo. This lesson profiles the major rivers, lakes and their socio-economic uses.
objectives: Explain why Ethiopia is called the Water Tower of Northeastern Africa
Compare the catchment areas and lengths of the major rivers
Describe the characteristics of Ethiopian rivers
Classify Ethiopian lakes into highland and Rift Valley lakes
State the socio-economic significances of rivers and lakes
g9-geography-ug3-t3.simple: Ethiopia has been known as the Water Tower of Northeastern Africa for the last fifty to sixty years, and it is the second richest African country in water resource potential, following the Democratic Republic of Congo. Ethiopian rivers are numerous and energetic: they flow from highlands to peripheral lowlands bouncingly, giving steep profiles, rapids, waterfalls and gorges, and their volume fluctuates seasonally. Major rivers include the Wabe Shebelle (2,000 km total), Abbay, Genale, Awash, Tekezze, Gibe/Omo and Baro, and some take new names abroad, like the Abbay becoming the Blue Nile in Sudan. Lakes are dispersed on plateaus and clustered in the Rift Valley, including Lake Tana (3,600 km2), Shalla (deepest at 266 m) and Ziway (shallowest at 4 m). Rivers and lakes supply hydropower, fishery, irrigation, navigation and tourism.
g9-geography-ug3-t3.detailed:
The Water Tower of Northeastern Africa. Ethiopia has been known as the Water Tower of Northeastern Africa for the last fifty to sixty years and is the second richest African country in terms of water resource potential, following the Democratic Republic of Congo. Ethiopia generally has adequate average annual rainfall in most areas, so it has several major rivers, lakes and significant ground water potentials. As well as being numerous, Ethiopian rivers are energetic: they flow from the highlands of the interior to the peripheral lowlands and then to seas and lakes bouncingly, which has made Ethiopia the watershed between the Mediterranean Sea and Indian Ocean drainage systems.

Major rivers and their data. The largest catchment area belongs to the Wabe Shebelle (205,407 km2; length 2,000 km, of which 1,340 km inside and 660 km outside), followed by the Abbay (198,508 km2; 1,360 km) with tributaries such as the Dabus, Didessa, Fincha, Guder, Muger and Jemma. The Genale drains 168,141 km2 (total length 1,050 km), the Awash 113,709 km2 (1,200 km, entirely within Ethiopia), the Tekezze 87,733 km2 (1,168 km), the Gibe/Omo 77,205 km2 (760 km, with the Gojeb and Gilgel Gibe tributaries) and the Baro 75,718 km2 (507 km, with the Akobo and Gilo).

Characteristics of Ethiopian rivers. Their most important characteristics are seasonal fluctuation in water volume, steep profiles as they arise from very high places and flow to the borders across lowlands, rapids and waterfalls along their courses, running through steep-sided river valleys and gorges, and serving as boundaries, both international and domestic. Because of the steep profiles, most rivers are not suitable for navigation.

New names abroad. Some rivers take new names after they cross the borders: River Abbay becomes the Blue Nile in Sudan; River Tekezze becomes River Athbara in Sudan; River Genale becomes River Juba in Somalia; and River Baro becomes River Sobat in Sudan.

Lakes of Ethiopia. By African standard, Ethiopia is a country rich in lakes, dispersed on the plateaus and clustered in the Rift Valley. Most lakes are the result of structures that occurred during the Quaternary Period, not outcomes of climate, which is proved by their location in the drier parts of the country. Highland lakes are crater or watershed lakes: a crater lake forms when an explosive volcano breaks a mountain open and the deep mouth fills with water; examples are Haik near Dessie and Hashenge near Korum, plus lakes around Bishoftu (Bishoftu, Kuriftu, Babbo Gaya, Arsedi), Wonchi and Dendi around Ambo, Ginchi and Wellisso, and Ziquala. A watershed lake forms when a sheet of lava dams up a shallow surface depression; Lake Tana, with an area of 3,600 km2 but a maximum depth of only 9 m, formed in the Quaternary when lava dammed the shallow depression between the Gojjam and Gondar Massif. Rift Valley lakes are clustered in a linear pattern along the floor of the Rift Valley, formed in depressions and basins caused by tectonic activities: Abbaya (1,160 km2, 13 m), Chamo (551 km2), Shalla (409 km2, the deepest lake at 266 m), Langano (230 km2, 46 m), Hawassa (229 km2), Abijatta (205 km2, 14 m) and Ziway (434 km2, the shallowest at 4 m).

Significance of rivers and lakes. First, hydropower generation: the Gibe (Gilgel Gibe 1, 2 and 3 plants), Awash (plants 1, 2 and 3), Fincha, Tekezze and Melka Wakena (Wabe Shebelle) plants, with Koysha and the Great Ethiopian Renaissance Dam under construction. Second, fishery, as with Lake Chamo, Lake Abbaya, Lake Tana and River Baro. Third, irrigation: the Awash is the most utilized because of the flat plains it crosses for hundreds of kilometers. Fourth, navigation: the Baro is the only river in Ethiopia used for water transport, while Lake Tana, Lake Ziway and Lake Abbaya are important inland water ways. Finally, tourism and recreation, from birds, fish and wildlife, deep gorges and all kinds of waterfalls; the economic potential is enormous but not well developed yet.

g9-geography-ug3-t3.summary: Ethiopia, the Water Tower of Northeastern Africa, is second to the Democratic Republic of Congo in water potential, with energetic rivers that fluctuate seasonally and fall through rapids and gorges toward neighbouring countries. The Wabe Shebelle leads both in length (2,000 km) and catchment (205,407 km2), and lakes divide into highland crater and watershed lakes, like Haik and Tana, and clustered tectonic Rift Valley lakes, like deepest Shalla (266 m). Rivers and lakes supply hydropower, fishery, irrigation, navigation and tourism for the country.

g9-geography-ug3-t4.overview: Soil is the loose material overlying the earth's crust that supports plants and animals, and Ethiopia's soils derive from volcanic, metamorphic and sedimentary rocks. This lesson explains soil formation and profiles the eight major soil types of Ethiopia.
objectives: Define soil and list its major components
Explain the factors responsible for soil formation in Ethiopia
Relate regional parent rocks to regional soil characters
Identify the eight major soil types and their locations
Compare the agricultural value of the main soil types
g9-geography-ug3-t4.simple: Soil is the loose material overlying the crust of the earth, consisting mainly of very small particles, with water, air, organic and inorganic minerals as its major components. Ethiopian soils result from parent rock, climate, vegetation cover and topography. On the volcanic plateaus red and black basaltic soils form; crystalline rocks give thin, rocky, acidic soils in Hararghe and Borena; Afar has shallow saline soils; the southeastern lowlands have humus-poor but phosphorus-rich soils; and river valleys hold fertile alluvial soils. The FAO recognizes 18 soil classes in Ethiopia; the main ones covering more than 85% of the country are Nithosols (red basaltic), Vertisols (black basaltic), Cambisols, Regosols, Xerosols, Luvisols, Lithosols and Fluvisols, with Nithosols the most widely cultivated.
g9-geography-ug3-t4.detailed:
What soil is and how it forms. Soil is the loose material overlying the crust of the earth consisting mainly of very small particles. Its major components are water, air, organic and inorganic minerals, and it is a dynamic, natural and complex substance which can support animals and plants. Soils of Ethiopia are the result of parent rock material broken into small particles by weathering and natural decomposition; climatic conditions, which determine the speed and nature of soil-forming processes, since extreme heat or cold can stop the work of bacteria and moisture influences soil formation; vegetation cover, which adds humus and supports soil-making animals and bacteria; and topography, since soils on side of hills tend to be shallow due to erosional losses.

Regional soil characters. On the plateaus of north, northwestern, southwestern, central and southeastern Ethiopia the parent rocks are volcanic and rainfall is sufficient, forming red basaltic and black basaltic soils; the black soils have high clay content that makes them difficult for farming. Where hard crystalline rocks are the parent material, soils are poor, thin, rocky and acidic, ranging from grey to brown, as in the Hararghe plateaus and Borena lowlands. In Afar, recent volcanic deposits and dried-out lake deposits give very shallow, saline-dominated soils. In the southeastern lowlands, sedimentary parent rocks give soils that lack humus but are rich in phosphorous and potash and low in nitrogen. In the lower courses of major rivers, fertile alluvial soils dominate because of their volcanic origin and continuous nourishment of water.

Nithosols (Red Basaltic Soils). These cover about 12% of the country, are associated with high rainfall and formerly forested areas, and are predominant in the Western Highlands of Wollega, Kafa and Illubabor, the Southern Highlands of Sidama, the Central and Western Highlands of Shewa, the Highlands of Gojjam and the Eastern Highlands of Hararghe. They are matured soils with deep profiles, highly leached, lacking soluble minerals like Sodium and Calcium but rich in iron and aluminum. Being friable with stable structure, they are potentially good for farming and are the most widely cultivated soil type, best for coffee, inset and cereals.

Vertisols (Black Basaltic Soils). These cover about 10% of Ethiopia's land, have high clay content so they are sticky, and their poor drainage makes them difficult for farming, though their excellent nutrients support agriculture and their use is largely for grazing. They are found in Arsi, Bale and central Hararghe, where there are pronounced wet and dry seasons.

The young and shallow soils. Cambisoils developed from the recent lava deposits of the Quaternary Period; they are young and shallow, on the rugged and sloping terrain of the Shewa Plateau (eastern escarpment) and the Chercher Highlands. Regosols are similar but coarse-textured, with low agricultural value, in the Danakil and Ogaden plains. Lithosols share the same poor maturity on steep slopes in areas of low precipitation, covering the escarpments of the Northeastern and Chercher Highlands.

Xerosols, Luvisols and Fluvisols. Xerosols are young and shallow soils of arid and semi-arid regions with weakly developed profiles, found extensively in the Northeastern escarpment and the Northwestern and Southeastern Lowlands; they have high salt content and humus deficiencies, so they matter for agriculture only where they can be irrigated. Luvisols are well developed where wet and dry seasons alternate and leaching is not very high; they are among the best soils with good chemical nutrients, intensively cultivated except on steep slopes or waterlogged areas, found around Lake Tana, in the eastern Northern Central Highlands and the Southern Lowlands. Fluvisols are soils that rivers have transported from highlands to lowlands, cover about 10% of the country, are associated with river, sea and lake deposits, and have very good agricultural potential, found extensively in the lower regions of the Omo, Awash, Abbay and Baro-Akobo Rivers.

g9-geography-ug3-t4.summary: Soil is a dynamic natural substance of water, air, organic and inorganic minerals, formed in Ethiopia from parent rock, climate, vegetation and topography, and derived from volcanic, metamorphic and sedimentary rocks. The FAO lists 18 classes, of which eight cover more than 85% of the country: Nithosols, Vertisols, Cambisols, Regosols, Xerosols, Luvisols, Lithosols and Fluvisols. Nithosols and Fluvisols are the farming favourites, while Vertisols, despite excellent nutrients, are hard to farm, and young shallow soils like Regosols and Xerosols have little agricultural value.

g9-geography-ug3-t5.overview: Geological surveys agree that Ethiopia holds many types of untapped mineral deposits, none yet extracted on a large scale. This lesson maps the metallic and non-metallic minerals and their distribution, from gold and platinum to potash and coal.
objectives: Describe the state of mineral exploitation in Ethiopia
Distinguish metallic from non-metallic minerals
Locate the major gold, platinum and tantalum deposits
Identify the non-metallic minerals and their areas
Relate mineral locations to geological environments
g9-geography-ug3-t5.simple: Preliminary geological survey shows that Ethiopia has many different types of untapped mineral deposition, and none is currently extracted on a large scale for commercial or industrial use. Non-metallic minerals are more produced annually than metallic ones and, except for common salt, production is small scale, though some minerals are exported. Metallic minerals include gold, found since ancient times in volcanic veins of Precambrian rocks and alluvial deposits, mined at Adola, Bule Hora, Arero, Moyale, Akobo, Lega Dembi, Sakaro and Tigray; platinum in the west (northeast Yubdo, north of Gimbi, the Akobo area); and tantalum at Kenticha, 50 km southeast of Shakiso in Adola. Non-metallics include potash and salt in the Danakil Depression (Dallol), soda ash in Lakes Abijatta and Shalla (460 million metric tons of Sodium Carbonate), limestone in Tigray, Shewa and Hararghe, clay widely, silica in several regions, crude oil and gas in the Ogaden basin, and lignite coal in Shewa, Sidama and Wollega.
g9-geography-ug3-t5.detailed:
The general picture. According to some preliminary geological survey, there is an agreement that Ethiopia has many different types of untapped mineral deposition. None of them is currently extracted on a large scale either for commercial or industrial use. In Ethiopia non-metallic minerals are more produced annually compared to the metallic ones, and with the exception of common salt, almost all other mineral production is small scale, though some amounts are exported.

Gold. Gold has been extracted in Ethiopia since ancient times from alluvial deposits. There are two principal geological environments in which gold is found: volcanic veins in Precambrian rocks and alluvial deposits. The largest active gold mines are Adola, Bule Hora, Arero, Moyale, Akobo, Lega Dembi, Sakaro and the Tigray regions.

Platinum and tantalum. Platinum is the key input for manufacturing of many electronic equipment including mobile phones. Its deposits are identified in the western parts of Ethiopia: northeast Yubdo, north of Gimbi, and in the Akobo area of Gambella region. Tantalum, like platinum, is used for manufacturing electronic equipment including mobile phones. Kenticha, a place 50 kms southeast of Shakiso in Adola, is identified as a tantalum rich area; in other areas of Adola tantalum bearing minerals have been found, but none of these areas has been explored in detail.

Potash, salt and soda ash. Potash and salt are found in the Danakil Depression (Dallol) area of the Northern Rift Valley, which is known for its rich potash and salt deposits. Geological surveys indicate that some Rift Valley lakes, namely Abijatta, Shalla and others, contain 460 million metric tons of Sodium Carbonate; the concentration of salt combined with a favorable climate makes this area potentially one of the best locations for soda ash production in the country.

Building and industrial minerals. Limestone is an important mineral resource for building and construction, used for the production of cement and chalk, with good reserves in Tigray, Shewa and Hararghe. Clay deposits are found in many parts of Ethiopia and are used for pottery and brick industries. Silica is an important raw material for glassy industries, with reserves of silica sand found in Harar, Shewa, Gondar, Gojjam, Sidamo, Arsi, Tigray and Wollega.

Fuel minerals. Reserves of natural gas and crude oil are believed to be found in the Ogaden basin. Lignite coal deposits are proved to exist in Shewa (Debre Brihan-Dessie road, Sululta and near Mojo), Sidama and Wollega. Together with the metallic and non-metallic list, these occurrences show that minerals, as non-renewable resources, still lie mostly beneath the surface awaiting detailed exploration.

g9-geography-ug3-t6.overview: Biotic resources are the living organisms of an ecosystem, and Ethiopia's natural vegetation and wildlife rank among its richest resources. This lesson maps the vegetation types by altitude and climate and profiles the wildlife, including endemic animals.
objectives: Define biotic resources and name their three categories
List the factors controlling the distribution of natural vegetation
Describe the four major vegetation types and where they occur
Classify Ethiopia's wildlife into its six broad categories
Identify endemic animals and explain why they are at risk
g9-geography-ug3-t6.simple: Biotic resources are living organisms in an ecosystem, sorted into producers (green plants), consumers (animals) and decomposers (bacteria and fungi). Natural vegetation, the original plant cover of an area, is controlled by altitude, climate, soil type and drainage; it follows altitude and rainfall closely. Ethiopia has four major vegetation types: Afroalpine and sub-Afroalpine on the Semein and Bale high mountains; forests between 450 and 3,300 m, divided into highland forests (Kerkha, Tid, Zigba, Woira, Kosso) and lowland gallery forests along the Awash, Wabe Shebelle and Genale; savanna woodland (250-2,300 m) with scattered acacias; and semi-desert xerophytes in the lowlands below 600 mm rainfall. Wildlife includes 277 mammals, 862 birds, 201 reptiles and 63 amphibians, with 7 mammals and 25 birds endemic, concentrated in the south and west.
g9-geography-ug3-t6.detailed:
Biotic resources. Biotic resources are living organisms in an ecosystem. They are typically sorted into three main categories: 1) producers, which include all green plants; 2) consumers, which include all animals; and 3) decomposers, which include bacteria and fungi. Natural vegetation, the original plant grown in and covering an area, is influenced by four most important factors: altitude, climate, soil type and drainage. In Ethiopia vegetation types correlate highly with altitude, rainfall and temperature: harsh lowlands with low rainfall bear xerophytic plants, while the highlands hold tree stands and forests.

Afroalpine and sub-Afroalpine vegetation. Known as high mountain vegetation, similar to European Alpine vegetation, it is found at very high altitudes: sub-Afroalpine between 3,000 and 3,300 m, and Afroalpine above 3,300 m above sea level. In Ethiopia these types are found in the Highlands of Semein and the Highlands of Bale. Afroalpine vegetation consists of tussock grasslands, scattered mosses and lichens; sub-Afroalpine vegetation is dominated by woodland scrubs, with Gibra (Lobelia rhynchopetalum) and Asta (Erica arborea) the dominant plant species.

Forests. Forests grow where altitude ranges from 450 to 3,300 m and total annual rainfall is between 200 and 2,200 mm, and this variation produces two very different forest types through altitudinal zonation. Highland forests (1,500-3,300 m) descend in belts: Kerkha (Arundinaria bamboo) at 2,800-3,000 m; Tid (Juniperus procera, coniferous) at 2,200-2,800 m; Zigba (Podocarpus) at 1,800-2,200 m; and Woira and Kosso at 1,500-1,800 m. Lowland forests below 1,500 m are gallery or riverine forests growing along the banks of the Awash, Wabe Shebelle and Genale Rivers where soil moisture is available, with Sholla and Warka predominant, and Baphia forest where mean annual rainfall exceeds 500 mm.

Savanna woodland. Savanna woodlands occur in both highland and lowland areas, from 250 to 2,300 m, with annual rainfall from 200 to 1,400 mm, and consist of grass mixed with scattered trees, shrubs and bush lands. They include Juniperus woodlands (mountain grasslands with Tid trees), Acacia woodlands (grasslands with Ghirar trees) and mixed deciduous woodlands (grasslands with Sholla and Warka). Savanna grasslands have marked seasons and scattered acacia trees, dominant at lower elevations and drier climates than forests; where mean annual rainfall exceeds 1,000 mm they form park-like areas with acacia, wild fig, sycamore and kosso trees, as in the southern half of Ziway, Langano, Abijatta and Hawassa areas.

Semi-desert and desert vegetation. In these regions xerophytes, drought-resisting plants, dominate: short acacia, thorn bushes, succulent plants and a few rough grasses. This vegetation is found in the Eastern (Afar) lowlands and the Northwestern and Southeastern (Ogaden) lowlands, where annual rainfall is below 600 mm and drought persists for a long period.

Wildlife of Ethiopia. Owing to Ethiopia's great environmental diversity in relief, climate and natural vegetation, the country is very rich in all kinds of wildlife: about 277 mammal species, 862 bird species, 201 reptile species and 63 amphibian species, of which 7 mammals and 25 birds are endemic. Wild animals are found in many parts of the country but largely concentrated in the south and west. The six broad categories are: common wild animals (hyenas, jackals) found in many places; game animals of the lowland grasslands, herbivore browsers like giraffes and grazers like wild ass and zebra, and carnivores like lion, leopard and cheetah; arboreal tree animals such as colobus monkey, apes and baboons of the rainforest regions; aquatic animals such as hippopotamus, fish and crocodiles; birds, both endemic and migratory, like fish eagles, pelicans, geese, the Abyssinian Ground Hornbill and flamingoes of the Rift Valley sanctuaries and forests; and endemic animals found only in Ethiopia: Walia Ibex in the Semein highlands, Mountain Nyala in the Bale Mountains, Gelada baboon in the Semein highlands, Menelik's Bushbuck in the Shewan and Bale highlands, Swayne's Hartebeest in Nechsar park and the Sankalle sanctuary, Semein Fox in the Bale and Semein highlands, and the Wild Ass of the Afar and Southeast lowlands. These rare animals, especially the Walia Ibex and Semein Fox, are approaching extinction.

keyTerms.def: A living organism in an ecosystem; sorted into producers, consumers and decomposers.
Any original plant grown in and covering an area, distributed by altitude, climate, soil type and drainage.
High mountain vegetation above 3,300 m, of tussock grasslands, mosses and lichens, in the Semein and Bale highlands.
Drought-resisting plants, such as short acacia, thorn bushes and succulents, of the lowland deserts and semi-deserts.
Lowland forest growing along river banks such as the Awash, Wabe Shebelle and Genale, with Sholla and Warka.
The ordering of vegetation into belts by altitude, seen in the forest trees Kerkha, Tid, Zigba, Woira and Kosso.
Wild animals found only in Ethiopia, such as the Walia Ibex, Mountain Nyala and Gelada baboon; they exist in small numbers and risk extinction.
Wild herbivores and carnivores of the lowland grasslands, including giraffe, zebra, lion, leopard and cheetah.

workedExamples.problem: Place the following vegetation types on an altitude profile from valley floor to summit: Afroalpine, savanna woodland, forest, semi-desert vegetation.
workedExamples.given: Semi-desert vegetation lies in lowlands below 600 mm rainfall; savanna woodland spans 250-2,300 m; forests span 450-3,300 m; Afroalpine lies above 3,300 m.
workedExamples.formula: Method: arrange vegetation belts by their recorded altitudinal ranges.
workedExamples.substitution: Lowest range: semi-desert lowlands. Then savanna woodland up to 2,300 m, then forest up to 3,300 m, then Afroalpine above 3,300 m.
workedExamples.calculation: Arranging by altitude gives one continuous belt for each type.
workedExamples.answer: Semi-desert vegetation (lowest), savanna woodland, forest, then Afroalpine on the Semein and Bale summits.

workedExamples.problem: A biologist records a hippopotamus, a colobus monkey and a lion in three different localities. Which wildlife category does each belong to?
workedExamples.given: The six categories are common, game, arboreal, aquatic, birds and endemic animals.
workedExamples.formula: Method: classify each animal by the habitat and habit stated in the textbook.
workedExamples.substitution: Hippopotamus lives in lakes and rivers; colobus monkeys climb trees in rainforests; lion is a carnivore game animal of the grasslands.
workedExamples.calculation: Each animal matches exactly one category.
workedExamples.answer: Hippopotamus - aquatic; colobus monkey - arboreal; lion - game animal (carnivore).

workedExamples.problem: An ecosystem contains green plants, hyenas, a lion, bacteria and fungi. Sort the organisms into producers, consumers and decomposers.
workedExamples.given: Producers include all green plants; consumers include all animals; decomposers include bacteria and fungi.
workedExamples.formula: Method: apply the three biotic categories to each organism listed.
workedExamples.substitution: Green plants produce; hyenas and lions consume; bacteria and fungi decompose.
workedExamples.calculation: Sorting leaves one category per group with none unaccounted for.
workedExamples.answer: Producers: green plants. Consumers: hyenas and lion. Decomposers: bacteria and fungi.

workedExamples.problem: A conservation plan must prioritize two animals it labels 'approaching extinction'. Which two endemic animals should be listed, and in which parks would rangers search?
workedExamples.given: The Walia Ibex lives in the Semein highlands and the Semein Fox in the Bale and Semein highlands; the Mountain Nyala lives in the Bale Mountains and Swayne's Hartebeest in Nechsar park and the Sankalle sanctuary.
workedExamples.formula: Method: match the risk level stated in the textbook to the animal and its location.
workedExamples.substitution: Walia Ibex - Semein highlands; Semein Fox - Bale and Semein highlands.
workedExamples.calculation: Both species are named as approaching extinction, so rangers must search the Semein and Bale highlands.
workedExamples.answer: The Walia Ibex and the Semein Fox; search the Semein highlands (and Bale for the fox), with other endemics safe-kept in Nechsar and Sankalle.

commonMistakes: Listing decomposers as a kind of consumer; bacteria and fungi form their own category.
Believing natural vegetation follows only rainfall; altitude, climate, soil type and drainage all act.
Confusing Afroalpine (above 3,300 m) with sub-Afroalpine (3,000-3,300 m) belts.
Placing gallery forests in the highlands; they are lowland riverine forests below 1,500 m.
Assuming wildlife is spread evenly; it is concentrated in the south and western parts of the country.
Saying drought is good for forests; dry areas below 600 mm carry only xerophytic semi-desert vegetation.
Forgetting that endemic animals exist in very small numbers and are at great risk of extinction.
applications: Planning a school expedition to see Afroalpine vegetation in the Bale or Semein mountains.
Explaining why agriculture and settlement replace original forests over most of the highlands.
Using vegetation maps to predict where national parks support game animals.
Reasoning why Rift Valley sanctuaries shelter both endemic and migratory birds.
Linking altitude belts (Kerkha, Tid, Zigba, Woira) to traditional timber choices.
Supporting campaigns that protect endemics like the Walia Ibex and Semein Fox from extinction.
g9-geography-ug3-t6.summary: Biotic resources are the living organisms of an ecosystem - producers, consumers and decomposers - and Ethiopia's natural vegetation follows altitude, climate, soil and drainage through four types: Afroalpine and sub-Afroalpine, forests, savanna woodland, and semi-desert vegetation. Wildlife includes about 277 mammals, 862 birds, 201 reptiles and 63 amphibians, with 7 mammal and 25 bird species endemic, concentrated in the south and west. Endemics like the Walia Ibex and Semein Fox live in very small numbers and risk extinction.
